chapters.title: Getting started
chapters.summary: What you are looking at, and where to begin.

blocks.text: You record what should be checked (test cases), carry those checks out (test runs), and read what came of it. Everything else — folders, suites, plans, reports — exists to keep those three things manageable.
Your landing page is the dashboard: a welcome banner, your queue of work waiting on you, and the projects you belong to.

items: Projects — each project is a self-contained area with its own test cases, runs and members.
My test runs — the runs you are named as executor on.
My bug reports — bug reports assigned to you, across all projects.
Watched — items you are notified about when they change.

blocks.text: You only see projects you are a member of. If one is missing, ask its administrator to add you.

chapters.title: Understanding roles
chapters.summary: Why you can see some things and not others.

items: Viewer — reads everything in the project, changes nothing.
Tester — writes and edits test cases, carries out runs, records results.
Administrator — additionally manages members and project settings.

blocks.text: Your role is per project. You can be a tester on one and only a viewer on another.
This manual only shows chapters that match your roles. If an instruction seems to be missing, you probably lack the role for it — ask the project administrator.

chapters.title: Reading test cases and results
chapters.summary: Understanding a test case, and reading a result correctly.

sections.heading: How a test case is built

blocks.text: A test case describes one check: a title, optional preconditions, and a sequence of steps. Each step has an action and an expected result — what should happen if all is well.

The status says how much weight it carries: Draft (still being written), In review (waiting for another member's approval, in projects that require review), Active (in use), Deprecated (no longer valid, kept for history).
Executing a case adds an actual result to each step. Expected and actual are always kept apart and labelled separately — comparing the two is the test result.

items: Passed — the actual matched the expected result.
Failed — it differed. That is a finding.
Blocked — the check could not be carried out, for instance because the environment was down. Also a finding: the case proved nothing.
Skipped — deliberately not checked. Not a finding.
Pending — not executed yet.

blocks.text: On a completed run the findings come first: results are ordered by urgency and failed entries are already expanded.
Every run has a report with figures, a chart and the full result list. The PDF button produces a version you can pass on.

The project's Activity page lists every change: who made it, when, and to what. An edit shows each changed field as old → new, and the entry links to the object while it exists. The History card on a test case, run, plan, suite or bug report shows that object's part, comments included.
Filter the Activity page by date range, person, kind of object and action, sort it newest or oldest first, and export what you see as CSV.

Compare with… on a run lists what changed against an earlier one: newly failing, fixed, still failing, added and removed test cases. The earlier run is picked for you — the previous run with the same name, or of the same plan and environment — and you can choose another.
A case marked "case edited" ran against different wording in the two runs, so its change may come from the test, not the product.

chapters.title: Writing test cases
chapters.summary: Recording, editing and versioning good test cases.

items: Open the project and go to Test cases.
Choose Create Test Case.
Give it a title — short, and phrased as a claim, e.g. "Login with valid credentials".
Record preconditions if the case needs a particular starting state.
Add steps: an action and an expected result for each.
Set priority and status, then save.

blocks.text: Write expected results you can actually check against. "Works" cannot be verified; "The confirmation page appears with the order number" can.
Every edit saves the previous wording as a version. The history shows what changed and when — which matters when a result refers to an older version of the case.
Replacing the step list discards screenshots attached to steps that no longer exist.

Steps you keep copying between cases, such as "Log in as admin", belong in a shared step. Create it under Shared steps on the project page. In a test case, on the Steps tab, choose Insert shared step: it appears as one row you can expand.

Editing a shared step changes every case that uses it, and runs started afterwards. The editor says how many cases that is; each keeps a version with its previous wording. On the test case page, Convert to local steps replaces the shared step with a copy the case owns.
A shared step can only be deleted while no case uses it.

Write placeholders in braces into the steps, such as "Log in as {user}", then add parameter sets under Parameters on the test case page, one per data combination. A run holds one result per set, with the values filled in.
A placeholder with no value in a set stays visible as written, and the editor warns you about it.

The Estimate on the Details tab is how many minutes one execution takes. Runs and plans add the estimates up to show the remaining effort, and the test case page shows the median actual time of its last five executions.

Files a tester needs to carry out the case, such as a sample file to upload or a spec PDF, go in the Attachments card on the test case page. Choose Attach file or drop a file onto the card. Images, PDF, ZIP, Office documents and text files up to 10 MB are accepted, and the content has to match the file type.
While executing a run, the case's attachments are listed above the steps, collapsed.
Attachments are not part of the version history. Adding or removing one shows in the project activity instead.

In a project that requires review, a case becomes Active only after another member approves it: finish it as a draft, choose Submit for review, and a reviewer approves it or requests changes. Changing the wording of an approved case sends it back to review; labels, priority and folder do not.
A project can add its own fields, such as Component or Sprint. They appear on the Details tab and can be used as filters. A field marked required has to be filled in before you save.

Edit as Gherkin on the Steps tab shows the case as one scenario in plain text, with Given, When and Then steps. Edit it and choose Apply to steps. It is not available while a case uses a shared step, because Gherkin has none.

chapters.title: Organising test cases
chapters.summary: Folders, suites, labels and plans — and when to use which.

items: Folders — a filing structure. A case sits in exactly one folder.
Suites — named groupings for a purpose, e.g. "Regression before release". A case may be in several suites.
Labels — free-form tags for filtering, e.g. "negative" or "accessibility".
Test plans — dated undertakings that group several runs together.

blocks.text: Reuse existing labels rather than inventing new ones. Two spellings of the same topic split the results and nobody notices.

Import on the test case list takes CSV, JSON or Gherkin .feature files, or a ZIP of .feature files, into a folder you choose. Always use Preview (dry run) first: it shows what would be created, updated or skipped, and saves nothing.
Export writes JSON, CSV, CSV for Excel, or Gherkin: the selected folder, or the whole project.

A Gherkin scenario tagged @tm: with a case key, such as @tm:SPI-17, updates that case instead of creating a new one. Export once to get the tags, keep those files, and import them again after changes.

chapters.title: Carrying out test runs
chapters.summary: From planning to a completed run.

items: In the project, go to Test runs and choose Start Test Run.
Give a name and an environment — the environment is what later explains what was tested against.
Select test cases, individually or via a suite.
Start. The run moves to In progress and the execution view opens.
Set a status per step and record the actual result.
Complete it once everything is recorded.

blocks.text: When something differs, record what actually happened, not just that it failed. "Error" helps nobody; "500 error after submitting" does.

When starting a run you pick its environment from the project's list, such as Staging. Run on multiple environments starts one run per environment. The test case page and plans then show the latest result per environment.

While a result is open in the execution view, a timer runs, and its time is saved with the result when you record the outcome. You can correct the duration by hand, for instance when you tested away from the screen.

For testing without scripted steps, start an exploratory session: a charter saying what to explore, a time box, and a log of notes as you go — observations, bugs, questions, ideas. Complete ends it with a debrief of what you covered and found.
A bug noted during a session can be reported directly from the note.
A completed or aborted run can be reopened with a reason. The reason is shown on the run, so it stays clear later why something was changed after the fact. Aborting asks for a reason too.

A screenshot can be attached to any step. As soon as a result or one of its steps is Failed or Blocked, you can report a bug from it, provided bug reports are switched on for the project; from a step, the bug names that step and takes its actual result. Link existing bug records that a known bug failed again here. With an issue tracker configured, you can also create and link an issue there directly, and the Defect link field holds a link to any other ticket.

chapters.title: Planning a release
chapters.summary: Test plans, their progress, and whether a release is ready.

blocks.text: A test plan gathers the runs for a milestone, such as a release, with a target date. Its page shows progress, the pass rate, results per environment and the runs themselves.

Every bug has a key such as SPI-BUG-12. New bugs start as New; Open means someone confirmed it. Closing a bug asks for a reason and a resolution, such as Fixed, Duplicate or Won't fix, and a duplicate names the bug it repeats.

In the Bug Reports list, search by key or text and filter by status, priority and assignee. Tick bugs to assign them, change their priority or status, or delete them in one step. The filters are in the URL, so a view can be bookmarked.
Dragging a card on the board to another lane asks for the reason first. Cancel, and the card stays where it was.
When the plan's test cases have estimates, the plan shows a burn-down: the remaining effort per day against an ideal line to the target date.

Editing a plan lets you set a release gate: a minimum effective pass rate, a maximum of open critical bugs, a minimum requirement coverage and a maximum of flaky tests. Release readiness on the plan then says GO or NO GO, criterion by criterion.
Leave a threshold empty to not use it. A CI pipeline can ask for the same verdict through the API before it deploys.

chapters.title: Notifications
chapters.summary: Keeping up with changes without watching everything.

blocks.text: The bookmark icon on a test run, test plan or bug report starts watching it. Changes then appear under the bell at the top right.
Notification settings control what you additionally hear about by e-mail.

items: Open the project and go to Members.
Add a member and choose their role.
Change the role later from the list, or remove the member.

blocks.text: Grant the smallest role that does the job. A role can always be raised; one granted too widely rarely gets noticed.
Under Requirements you record what the product must do and link the test cases that demonstrate it. The coverage matrix then shows which requirements are actually proven.
Watch for the "untested" status: a requirement with a linked case that has never run. Covered on paper, demonstrated by nothing.
The project page's Project Settings are where a project is shaped:

items: Bug reports — switches the built-in bug tracker on. Once it is on, the bug report template sets the text and default environment new bug reports start with.
Test case review — cases become Approved only after another member reviews them. Choose whether only project admins or testers too may approve.
Manage environments — the list runs and bug reports pick from. Renaming keeps the history; archive an environment instead of deleting it.
Manage custom fields — extra typed fields on test cases, runs and bug reports: text, number, date, or one or several options.

blocks.text: Webhooks send events to other systems, with ready-made formats for Slack, Microsoft Teams and Mattermost. An issue tracker — GitLab, GitHub, Jira, Forgejo or Linear — lets testers create and link an issue straight from a failed result.

chapters.title: Administering the instance
chapters.summary: Users, sign-in, API keys and build servers.

blocks.text: Settings is where you manage user accounts and optionally set up single sign-on. Without SSO, users sign in with an e-mail address and password.
An API key belongs to exactly one project and holds a role there: viewer reads, tester may write. The key is shown once.

items: Regenerate replaces the secret. Project, role and history stay; the old key stops working immediately.
Revoke additionally removes the key's project membership.
Regenerate as soon as a key has turned up anywhere it should not have.

blocks.text: A CI pipeline reports results back through the external interface — JUnit XML, Cucumber JSON or plain JSON, authenticated with an API key.

curl -X POST https://<host>/api/external/projects/<PROJECT>/test-runs/junit \
  -H 'X-API-Key: tm_…' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' \
  --data-binary @surefire.xml
Cucumber results land on the test case whose @tm: tag the scenario carries, even after the scenario was renamed; untagged scenarios are matched by name.
An MCP server can also be switched on, letting an AI agent create test cases, suites and plans. It is off by default; every call is recorded and visible under MCP activity.

The database holds everything, attachments and screenshots included. On the server, ./scripts/backup.sh writes a dump, and ./scripts/restore.sh restores one into an empty database; the chapter "Installation and operations" in docs/USER_MANUAL.md has the details.

./scripts/backup.sh
./scripts/restore.sh backups/testmanagement-<timestamp>-V64.dump
Back up the .env file separately and just as carefully. Without APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY, stored issue-tracker and build-server tokens and SSO secrets have to be entered again.
